title: A quick prayer, then speak (Nehemiah 2:1–5)
hookLine: the king's cupbearer prays silently, then makes his request
carry: the slow work was done before

lines: NEWS FROM HOME: THE WALL IS DOWN.
cards: A cup of wine is on its way to a king. The man carrying it is Nehemiah, a Jew in exile, cupbearer to King Artaxerxes of Persia, in the palace at Shushan. He says he had never been sad in the king's presence before.

But he has heard news from home: the wall of Jerusalem is broken down and its gates burned with fire. He wept, the book says, and fasted, and prayed. Now he hands over the cup, and the king sees his face.
Why is your face sad, the king asks, when you aren't sick? This is nothing but sorrow of heart. Nehemiah writes that he was very much afraid.

teach.h: AN HONEST ANSWER TO THE KING.
teach.b: Nehemiah answers honestly. Let the king live forever; why shouldn't my face be sad, when the city where my fathers are buried lies waste and its gates are burned?

teach.h: SO I PRAYED TO THE GOD OF HEAVEN.
teach.b: Then the king asks, in the King James words: "For what dost thou make request? So I prayed to the God of heaven." And the very next words: "And I said unto the king."
No kneeling, no long speech. The king is waiting, and between the question and the answer Nehemiah prays. The book doesn't tell us the words.
What it shows is the order: a quick prayer, then speak. And it isn't his only prayer. In chapter one he prayed at length, with fasting, confession and a long plea.
The slow work was done before; the short prayer is what fits in the gap.

Then Nehemiah speaks, and he's specific. If it please the king, send me to Judah, to the city of my fathers' graves, that I may build it. He asks for letters for safe passage and for timber from the king's forest.

And the king grants it, the text says, according to the good hand of God upon him. Today the king might be a manager, a doctor, a landlord, a parent. The gap between their question and your answer is short.
Nehemiah shows what can fit inside it.

how: Jewish tradition has set prayers for fixed times, and also short, personal prayers said in the moment; Nehemiah's silent prayer before answering the king is sometimes pointed to as an example of the second kind.

o: a steward who kept the keys to the king's treasury
a priest who carried the cup in the Temple
the servant who poured and served the king's wine

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.

s: the text gives the words of Nehemiah's quick prayer
it only says "so I prayed to the God of heaven," then he speaks.
Nehemiah had already prayed at length before this moment
in chapter one he wept, fasted and prayed when he heard the news.
Nehemiah hid his sadness from the king
the king saw his sad face and asked about it.

games.q: you're Nehemiah. the king has just asked, "for what dost thou make request?" the cup is in his hand. what do you do?
o: ask for time to think it over.
pray silently, then make a clear request.
games.why: "so I prayed to the God of heaven. and I said unto the king": a prayer in the gap, then a specific ask to go and build.

practice: Bring to mind one request you need to make soon, a day off, help with something, a hard conversation, and see the person you'll ask.
Take one breath in the gap, turning to God in it if you pray, or just letting it steady you if you don't, then say the ask plainly in your mind, in a sentence or two.

wordCard.voice: Cupbearer, Nehemiah's role serving King Artaxerxes, the position he held when he prayed a quick prayer and then spoke. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: so I prayed to the God of heaven, Nehemiah 2:4.

carryVoice: Your line: the slow work was done before. The quick prayer stood on a long one. See you tomorrow.
